title: Visualizing Proximal Policy Optimization from Scratch with Cart‑Pole
description: Balance a pole on a cart using deep reinforcement learning, all running on your laptop — no cloud, no strings attached.
content:
<!-- Based on the following repo: [Cart-Pole-PPO](https://github.com/thatrandomfrenchdude/cart-pole-ppo). -->
 
## 🔍 Introduction
Imagine watching a neural agent learn to balance a pole in real time. This project couples a custom cart‑pole environment in Python with a PPO agent in PyTorch and a live web‑based visualisation. By the end of the tutorial, you’ll have a fully working, local application that can run a pre‑trained PPO model or train a new one from scratch.

## 🌍 Why Edge?
Running everything locally means no latency from API calls and no unnecessary dependencies. Instead, the Flask server serves the API and static files directly from your machine, and training occurs in a separate thread.

Edge computing pushes computation to the device, reducing bandwidth and improving privacy -- perfect for iterating on reinforcement learning experiments without sending data to the cloud. While it may not matter much in this scenario, it sets the stage for more complex applications where data privacy and real-time processing are crucial.

## ⚙️ Prerequisites & Setup
- Python 3.8+ with pip; alternatively, use Docker.
- Clone the repo and create a virtual environment:

    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/thatrandomfrenchdude/cart-pole-ppo.git
    cd cart-pole-ppo
    python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate  # Windows: venv\\Scripts\\activate
    pip install -r requirements.txt
    pip install -r requirements-test.txt  # for tests [oai_citation:6‡github.com]
    # optional: pip install onnxruntime-qnn  # for Qualcomm NPU acceleration
    ```
- Run tests to ensure the environment is correctly configured:

    ```bash
    pytest
    ```

## 🛠️ Step‑by‑Step Implementation

**Step 1 – Initialise the Project**

Set up the project as above and familiarise yourself with the structure. The core logic lives in `src/agent.py` (PPO implementation) and `src/environment.py` (custom cart‑pole environment).

**Step 2 – Run in Example Mode**

Launch the application server:

```bash
python main.py  # or docker-compose up
```

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. A pre‑trained model balances the cart‑pole, and the web UI displays live metrics.

**Step 3 – Switch to Training Mode**

To train your own agent, edit `config.yaml` and set `training.example_mode` to `false`. Then run `python main.py` again. The PPO algorithm will start collecting experiences, updating the policy every 200 steps and logging rewards.

**Step 4 – Explore Model Formats and Conversion**

Experiment with different model formats. Pre‑trained models are available as PyTorch, TorchScript and ONNX files in the example folder. Use `src/aihub_conversion.py` to convert .pth files to .pt and .onnx for NPU acceleration. You can compare inference speed using `src/compare_models.py`.

## 📊 Results & Testing
Before training, run the comprehensive test suite with pytest or the provided scripts to ensure all components work as expected. Then, launch the training.

While training, monitor the average reward in the terminal or via the web UI. Cart‑Pole is considered solved when the average reward exceeds 195 over 100 episodes. On average, this should be achieved in about 30 mins with 300 episodes.

## 📱 Edge Considerations & Performance
Because training and inference run at the edge on your device, you get immediate feedback with low latency without an internet connection. Plus, the modular architecture keeps the web server responsive by running training in a separate thread.

Once trained, you can optionally offload inference to a Snapdragon NPU via ONNX conversion using AI hub with the provided `src/aihub_conversion.py` script. 

## 🧠 Conclusion
You now have a working reinforcement learning pipeline with a built‑in visualiser that runs entirely on your machine. Try tweaking the environment physics or PPO hyperparameters in `config.yaml`, convert models for mobile inference, or even port the environment to another language. Share your results or fork the repo to add new features—happy balancing!

- **Model Comparison Script** – Use `src/compare_models.py` to benchmark inference speed across formats.
